sources.title: Phan Huy Lê: Thăng Long’s imperial citadel and its historical significance
sources.note: Historian’s conference study, reprinted by Vietnam National Museum of History. Direct text: opening chronology, 1010 move, Lý/Trần/Hồ/Ming/Lê/Mạc phases and 1802 Huế capital. Dates describe different regimes and functions, not continuous independent rule. Do not reuse its incorrect square-meter rendering of the site area.

sources.title: Vietnam National Museum of History: Đại Việt’s name in 1054
sources.note: Direct museum-hosted Vũ Tiến Đức article, section Những năm Ngọ ý nghĩa về nội trị. Used only 1054 Lý Thánh Tông change and Hồ-era Đại Ngu exception. Its total of 723 years and claims of instant 1786 reunification are not used.

sources.title: UNESCO: Central Sector of the Imperial Citadel of Thang Long
sources.note: Direct Outstanding Universal Value: eleventh-century Lý construction over earlier fortress on reclaimed delta land; excavated layers and influences from China and Champa. Seven-century predecessor not presented as Đại Việt.

sources.title: Vietnam National Museum of History: The 1288 campaign and Bạch Đằng
sources.note: Direct Nguyễn Thúy museum synthesis, paragraphs on loss of grain convoy, temporary occupation of Thăng Long and tidal stakes. Only basic campaign mechanism used; inflated troop totals, total-destruction rhetoric and precise casualty claims excluded. Mirror baotanglichsu.vn is same work.

sources.title: Vietnam National Museum of History: Đông Quan agreement and Ming withdrawal
sources.note: Direct account: December 1427 agreement, supplies for departing army, final January 1428 departure and Lê establishment. No reproduction of nationalistic rhetoric or unverified army totals.

sources.title: Nguyễn Ngọc Chất: Reassessing the Mạc dynasty
sources.note: Museum historian’s direct article. Used retrospective bias toward Hồ/Mạc/Tây Sơn and Mạc continuation of examinations. Erroneous name of the king deposed in 1527, sweeping prosperity claims and questionable shipwreck dating are not adopted.

sources.title: Vietnam National Museum of History: Thăng Long in the Tây Sơn era
sources.note: Direct opening and 1786 to 1789 political narrative: Trịnh/Nguyễn warfare, divided north/south, Tây Sơn overthrow of Trịnh and Quang Trung’s defeat of Qing army. No army totals, disputed calendar conversions or claim of stable nationwide unification in 1786.

sources.title: Thăng Long heritage authority: Ancient wells in the Imperial Citadel
sources.note: Direct paragraphs 3 to 8: Lý reuse of earlier wells, Trần herringbone brickwork, no adhesive, small wells interpreted ritually. The 26-well count spans several periods and is not used as a Trần-only total. Claims that groundwater was inherently healthier omitted.

sources.title: Vietnam National Museum of History: White-glazed Lý and Trần ceramics, eleventh to fourteenth centuries
sources.note: Direct collection study: kiln waste from Thăng Long, fused bowls/plates; Bát subsection diameter 16.5 cm and five support scars. Do not classify all decorated vessels as ordinary household possessions or ritual cups as food cups.

sources.title: Asian Civilisations Museum: Vietnamese dish, accession 1995-02504
sources.note: Direct National Heritage Board catalogue. Fifteenth/sixteenth century flying duck and water rushes, cobalt underglaze, 22.6 cm diameter; paragraph on Southeast Asian markets. Inconsistent material metadata says porcelain while prose identifies stoneware, so public copy calls it ceramic. No invented excavation provenance.

sources.title: UNESCO: Hội An Ancient Town
sources.note: Direct Outstanding Universal Value, brief synthesis and authenticity: fifteenth to nineteenth century port; seventeenth/eighteenth century townscape, many structures renewed nineteenth century. Street customers and river loading, timber houses, markets and family cult houses. No claim every surviving structure is medieval.

sources.title: Temple of Literature nomination to UNESCO: Stone Stele Records of Royal Examinations
sources.note: Direct PDF pages 1 and 3, 82 steles erected 1484 to 1780, recording exams 1442 to 1779; turtle bases and inscriptions. Page 6 regular triennial exams and title Tiến sĩ. Unreliable typographical dates/royal names elsewhere in nomination not used.

sources.title: Institute of Hán-Nôm Studies: Inscription for the 1463 examination, erected 1484
sources.note: Vietnam Academy of Social Sciences scholarly transcription with Vietnamese translation. Direct original text paragraph begins 光順四年癸未科進士題名碑記; sample 人才國家之元氣 in 皇上特念 clause. End dates erection 洪德十五年八月十五日, 1484. Exam/banquet descriptions in opening. Mistaken royal footnote and later biographical typos excluded. This is Đào Cử’s 1463-exam stele, not Thân Nhân Trung’s better-known 1442-exam stele.

sources.title: Nguyễn Hữu Giới: The physician Lê Hữu Trác and his medical books
sources.note: Direct Vietnam National Museum of History reproduction of author’s Báo Văn Hóa article, 27 February 2026. Family return, nickname, schooling, manuscript copying and fields covered. Uncertain 1781 court-visit date and claim of first printing in 1885 not repeated; no efficacy claim or treatment advice.

sources.title: Vietnam National Archives: Nguyễn administration and the 1802 to 1804 transition
sources.note: Direct scholarly article hosted by national archives. Opening paragraphs: Nguyễn Phúc Ánh reunification in 1802, name Việt Nam in 1804 and Gia Long reign 1802 to 1820. Later Minh Mạng administrative reforms are outside this imported record and omitted.

proposedOverrides.summary: Successive Vietnamese royal states connected the Red River heartland with changing southern territories, through periods of unity and divided rule.

batchIdentityNotes.finding: Exact indexed ID Đại Việt, alias Annam, imported 1100 to 1815. Missing in runtime/overrides and no staged collision at claim. Decoded snapshots saved in identities.json. Identical broad 1530 to 1815 footprint masks rival governments and warfare; public overview warns against unified-territory interpretation. Dynastic sequence is a narrative for this imported label, not an assertion of one unbroken polity. No aliasing to modern Viet Nam, Champa, or separately indexed dynasties. From/to remain map coverage, ending is transformation; fell and successors omitted to preserve any curated transition.
